'''Richard Allen Jefferson Jr.''' (born June 21, 1980) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player who played [[small forward]]. He played for eight teams during his 17-season career in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA).

Jefferson played [[college basketball]] for the [[Arizona Wildcats men's basketball|Arizona Wildcats]], and was selected with the 13th overall pick in the first round by the [[New Jersey Nets]] in the [[2001 NBA draft]]. He was named to the [[NBA All-Rookie Second Team]] following his first season. Jefferson played seven seasons for the Nets, reaching the NBA Finals in each of his first two seasons. He later played for the [[Milwaukee Bucks]], [[San Antonio Spurs]], [[Golden State Warriors]], [[Utah Jazz]], [[Dallas Mavericks]], [[Cleveland Cavaliers]], and [[Denver Nuggets]]. He won an [[NBA Finals|NBA championship]] with the Cavaliers in [[2016 NBA Finals|2016]] and a bronze medal as a member of the [[United States men's national basketball team|United States national team]] in the [[2004 Summer Olympics]]. Jefferson retired from the NBA in 2018, becoming a basketball analyst for [[ESPN]] in 2019.

==Early life==
Jefferson was born in Los Angeles and was raised in [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]]. His mother and stepfather were both Christian [[missionaries]], and he moved around frequently growing up.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Growing Up ... Richard Jefferson |url=https://www.nba.com/cavaliers/news/features/growingup-jefferson-151011 |access-date=2022-12-02 |website=Nba.com |language=en}}</ref> Jefferson attended [[Moon Valley High School]] in [[Maryvale (Phoenix)|West Phoenix]], where he was an integral part of the varsity basketball team that won the 4A State Championship in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/sports/high-school/2016/09/23/richard-jefferson-brings-nba-championship-trophy-his-alma-mater-moon-valley-high-school/90921326/|title=Richard Jefferson brings NBA championship trophy to his alma mater Moon Valley High School|first=Richard|last=Obert|website=The Arizona Republic}}</ref>

==College career==
Jefferson played college basketball at the [[Arizona Wildcats men's basketball|University of Arizona]], under Hall of Fame coach [[Lute Olson]] from 1998 to 2001. During his 84-game career (77 starts), Jefferson averaged 11.2 points, 5.0 rebounds and 2.8 assists per game. He capped his career by being part of the Arizona team that advanced to the 2001 national championship game where the Wildcats fell to Duke. Along the way, Jefferson was an all-Midwest Regional and all-Final Four selection.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.arizonawildcats.com/facilities/richard-jefferson-gym.html|title=ArizonaWildcats.com - University of Arizona Athletics|website=Arizonawildcats.com}}</ref> He was inducted into the [[Pac-12 Basketball Hall of Honor]] during the [[2012 Pac-12 Conference men's basketball tournament]] on March 10, 2012.<ref>[http://www.pac-12.org/BasketballM/Tabid/1449/Article/143110/2011-12-Hall-of-Honor-Class-Announced.aspx 2011-12 Hall of Honor Class Announced] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120212101811/http://www.pac-12.org/BasketballM/Tabid/1449/Article/143110/2011-12-Hall-of-Honor-Class-Announced.aspx |date=February 12, 2012 }}, Pac-12 Conference, February 7, 2012</ref>

==Professional career==

===New Jersey Nets (2001–2008)===
Jefferson played seven seasons with the [[New Jersey Nets]] and was a key element of their back-to-back Eastern Conference Championship teams of 2002 and 2003. He played in the NBA Finals with the Nets in each of his first two seasons.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/668465/2018/11/21/qa-richard-jefferson-reflects-on-his-nets-tenure-clubbing-in-new-york-and-other-valuable-stops-in-his-career/|title=Q&A: Richard Jefferson reflects on his Nets tenure, clubbing in New York and other valuable stops in his career|first=Michael|last=Scotto|website=The Athletic}}</ref> In addition, Jefferson was a member of the USA Men's Olympic basketball team in the [[2004 Summer Olympics]]. Jefferson competed in the [[NBA Slam Dunk Contest]] in 2003.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-02-19 |title=Richard Jefferson |url=https://olympics.com/en/athletes/richard-jefferson |access-date=2024-02-19 |website=olympics.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=ESPN.com: NBA - Dunk contest soars as Richardson outshines Mason |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/allstar/2003/news/2003/0208/1506224.html |access-date=2024-02-19 |website=Espn.com}}</ref>

Jefferson began his career as a substitute [[small forward]] for [[Keith Van Horn]] and showed great defensive skills and all-around ability. Because of his potential, and Van Horn's conflict with [[power forward (basketball)|power forward]] [[Kenyon Martin]], the Nets traded Van Horn to the [[Philadelphia 76ers]] and trusted Jefferson as a starter. Jefferson blossomed in the role, becoming a good mid- and long-range shooter in addition to his slashing ability. On August 13, 2004, Jefferson signed a six-year, $78,000,000 contract extension with the Nets.

Jefferson missed the majority of the [[2004–05 NBA season|2004–05 regular season]] after rupturing a [[ligament]] in his left [[wrist]], an injury he claimed occurred when [[Detroit Pistons]] guard [[Chauncey Billups]] purposely undercut him on a layup attempt during a game on December 27, 2004. Jefferson ended up missing 49 games, but returned to action for the first round of the playoffs against the [[Miami Heat]]. Prior to suffering the injury, he had missed only five games in his three NBA seasons. Jefferson had been enjoying his best professional season, averaging 22.2 points, 7.3 rebounds, and 4.0 assists per game. Through the [[2005–06 NBA season|2005–06 season]], Jefferson continued to perform at a high level and established himself as one of the NBA's most versatile players. On January 21, 2007, Jefferson decided to have ankle surgery.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/22/sports/basketball/22nets.html|title=Nets Will Lose Jefferson for 6 Weeks|first=John|last=Eligon|newspaper=The New York Times|date=September 13, 2017}}</ref> After missing around six weeks, he was back in the lineup. His absence proved to be a major setback for the struggling Nets, who surged back into playoff contention once Jefferson returned.

In August 2007, Jefferson pledged $3.5 million toward the University of Arizona's then-planned basketball and volleyball practice facility, which was eventually named in his honor.<ref>{{cite web|title=Richard Jefferson Gymnasium|work=arizonawildcats.com|url=https://arizonawildcats.com/facilities/richard-jefferson-gymnasium-m-w-basketball-and-volleyball-/13}}</ref>

Jefferson started the 2007–08 season in the best form of his NBA career. In the first 7 games, he averaged 26.9 points, 5.6 rebounds and 2.4 assists, while also notching up 1.3 steals, 97.1% in free-throws and 49.1% in field-goals. On October 31, in a game against the Chicago Bulls, Jefferson injured his right wrist slightly, thumping his chest following a clutch three-pointer. The Nets went on to win the game in overtime. On December 4 he passed [[Kerry Kittles]] to become the Nets' second all-time leading scorer.

===Milwaukee Bucks (2008–2009)===
On June 26, 2008, Jefferson was traded to the [[Milwaukee Bucks]] for [[Yi Jianlian]] and future teammate [[Bobby Simmons]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/bucks/news/jefferson_for_yi_and_simmons_080626.html|title=Bucks acquire Richard Jefferson from New Jersey for Bobby Simmons and Yi Jianlian|website=THE OFFICIAL SITE OF THE MILWAUKEE BUCKS}}</ref> He was unhappy with the trade at first because he planned on being a Net until retirement. However, Jefferson later expressed enthusiasm about playing alongside [[Michael Redd]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/nba_news/jefferson_trade_080707.html|title=NBA.com Jefferson Says He Likes Trade to Milwaukee|website=Nba.com}}</ref>

===San Antonio Spurs (2009–2011)===
[[File:Richard Jefferson Spurs.jpg|thumb|Jefferson in 2011]]
On June 23, 2009, Richard Jefferson was traded to the [[San Antonio Spurs]] for [[Bruce Bowen]], [[Kurt Thomas (basketball)|Kurt Thomas]], and [[Fabricio Oberto]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/spurs/news/090623_jefferson.html|title=Spurs Obtain Richard Jefferson|website=Spurs.com}}</ref>

On June 30, 2010, Jefferson opted out of his contract with San Antonio and became an unrestricted free agent. On July 23, Jefferson re-signed with the Spurs.

===Golden State Warriors (2012–2013)===
[[File:Richard Jefferson Warriors.jpg|thumb|Jefferson in 2013|left|338x338px]]
On March 15, 2012, the [[Golden State Warriors]] traded the newly acquired [[Stephen Jackson]] for Jefferson, along with a conditional first-round pick.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/7691112/golden-state-warriors-trade-stephen-jackson-san-antonio-spurs |title=Spurs acquire Stephen Jackson |agency=Associated Press |access-date=March 15, 2012}}</ref>

===Utah Jazz (2013–2014)===
On July 5, 2013, the Warriors reportedly agreed to trade Jefferson, along with teammates [[Brandon Rush]] and [[Andris Biedriņš]], as well as two first-round picks and two second round picks, to the [[Utah Jazz]] in a three team deal, in which they received [[Andre Iguodala]] from the [[Denver Nuggets]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://philadelphia.cbslocal.com/2013/07/05/ap-sources-warriors-clear-space-acquire-iguodala/|title=AP Sources: Warriors Clear Space, Acquire Iguodala|date=July 5, 2013}}</ref> The trade became official five days later.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/warriors/news/warriors-acquire-andre-iguodala-071013|title=Warriors Acquire Andre Iguodala from Denver Nuggets as Part of Three-Team Trade|work=NBA.com|date=July 10, 2013|access-date=July 10, 2013}}</ref>

===Dallas Mavericks (2014–2015)===
On July 21, 2014, Jefferson signed with the [[Dallas Mavericks]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mavs.com/mavs-sign-richard-jefferson/|title=Mavs Sign Richard Jefferson|work=mavs.com|date=July 21, 2014|access-date=July 21, 2014}}</ref> He was the last Maverick to wear #24 before it was retired in honor of [[Mark Aguirre]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/teams/DAL/numbers.html|title=Dallas Mavericks Uniform Numbers|website=Basketball-reference.com|access-date=July 11, 2026}}</ref>.

===Cleveland Cavaliers (2015–2017)===
On August 5, 2015, Jefferson signed with the [[Cleveland Cavaliers]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/cavaliers/releases/jefferson-signing-2015|title=Cavs Sign Forward Richard Jefferson|work=NBA.com|date=August 5, 2015|access-date=August 5, 2015}}</ref> On October 27, he made his Cavaliers debut, recording 10 points, an assist, and a steal in a narrow 97–95 loss to the [[Chicago Bulls]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cleveland Cavaliers vs Chicago Bulls Oct 27, 2015 Game Summary|url=https://www.nba.com/game/0021500002|access-date=December 26, 2021|website=NBA}}</ref> The Cavaliers finished the regular season with a 57–25 record and reached the [[2016 NBA Finals]] with a 12–2 playoff record. During the third NBA Finals of his career, Jefferson played in every game of the series, including two starts in place of the injured [[Kevin Love]]. During Game 3, Jefferson gave the Cavaliers a boost in 33 minutes, posting nine points and eight rebounds as the Cavaliers cut the [[Golden State Warriors]]' advantage in the series to 2–1 with a 120–90 victory.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/games/20160608/GSWCLE/gameinfo.html|title=LeBron scores 32, Cavs wallop Warriors 120-90 in Game 3|work=NBA.com|date=June 8, 2016|access-date=June 13, 2016}}</ref> Despite falling into a 3–1 deficit, the Cavaliers completed the historic comeback to take the series in seven games, winning Jefferson his first and only championship.[[File:Richard Jefferson (37560571152).jpg|thumb|Jefferson in 2017]]After initially considering retirement following the championship win, Jefferson re-signed with the Cavaliers on July 28, 2016,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/cavaliers/releases/jefferson-signing-2016|title=Cavaliers Re-Sign Forward Richard Jefferson|work=NBA.com|date=July 28, 2016|access-date=July 28, 2016}}</ref> reportedly on a two-year, $5 million contract.<ref>{{cite web|last=Fedor|first=Chris|url=http://www.cleveland.com/cavs/index.ssf/2016/07/cavs_officially_re-sign_vetera.html|title=Cavs officially re-sign veteran Richard Jefferson|work=Cleveland.com|date=July 28, 2016|access-date=October 26, 2016}}</ref> The Cavaliers returned to the NBA Finals in [[2017 NBA Finals|2017]], but fell short in their quest for back-to-back titles, losing in five games to the Warriors. In his final game with the Cavaliers, Jefferson logged four points and two rebounds in a 129–120 road loss to the Warriors.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cleveland Cavaliers vs Golden State Warriors Jun 12, 2017 Game Summary|url=https://www.nba.com/game/0041600405|access-date=December 26, 2021|website=NBA}}</ref>

On October 14, 2017, Jefferson was traded, along with [[Kay Felder]], two future second-round draft picks and cash considerations, to the [[Atlanta Hawks]] in exchange for the rights to [[Sergiy Gladyr]] and [[Dimitrios Agravanis]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/cavaliers/releases/trade-171014|title=Cavaliers Complete Trade with Atlanta|work=NBA.com|date=October 14, 2017|access-date=October 14, 2017}}</ref> He was immediately waived by the Hawks.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/hawks/hawks-acquire-felder-and-jefferson|title=Hawks Acquire Draft Picks and Cash Considerations From Cavs|work=NBA.com|date=October 14, 2017|access-date=October 14, 2017}}</ref>

===Denver Nuggets (2017–2018)===
On October 19, 2017, Jefferson signed a one-year, $2.3 million contract with the [[Denver Nuggets]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/nuggets/news/nuggets-sign-richard-jefferson-101917|title=Nuggets Sign Richard Jefferson|work=NBA.com|date=October 19, 2017|access-date=October 19, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Wojnarowski |first=Adrian |url=http://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/21045715/richard-jefferson-agrees-1-year-deal-denver-nuggets|title=Richard Jefferson agrees to one-year, $2.3M deal with Nuggets|work=ESPN|date=October 17, 2017|access-date=October 19, 2017}}</ref>

=== Retirement ===
On October 13, 2018, Jefferson announced his retirement from professional basketball.<ref>{{cite web|title=Richard Jefferson retires after 17 NBA seasons|url=http://www.nba.com/article/2018/10/13/richard-jefferson-announces-retirement|work=NBA.com|access-date=October 13, 2018|date=October 13, 2018}}</ref>

==Broadcasting career==
{{Infobox sports announcer|name=Richard Jefferson|image=Richard Jefferson Broadcasting for Yes Network.jpg|caption=Jefferson broadcasting from the [[Barclays Center]] in 2025|genre=[[Color commentary]]|sport=[[NBA]]|employer=* [[YES Network]]
* [[ESPN]]|years_active=2018–present}}

On October 16, 2018, Jefferson joined the [[YES Network]] as the Nets' game and studio analyst.<ref>{{cite web |title=Former Net Richard Jefferson joins YES Network as Brooklyn Nets Analyst |url=https://www.nba.com/nets/news/2018/10/16/former-net-richard-jefferson-joins-yes-network-brooklyn-nets-analyst |website=NBA.com |access-date=October 17, 2018 |date=October 16, 2018}}</ref> He has also appeared as a basketball analyst on [[Fox Sports 1|FS1]] and the [[Pac-12 Network]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pac-12.com/news/2018/11/9/pac-12-networks-announces-roster-air-broadcasters-and-expert-analysts-2018-19.aspx|title = Pac-12 Networks announces roster of on-air broadcasters and expert analysts for 2018-19 season of men's and women's basketball coverage|website=pac-12.com| date=November 9, 2018 }}</ref> In 2019, Jefferson joined [[ESPN]] as an NBA analyst.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://espnpressroom.com/us/bios/richard-jefferson/|title=Richard Jefferson|website=espnpressroom.com|access-date=March 31, 2024}}</ref>

During the 2017 season, Jefferson began co-hosting the podcast ''Road Trippin''' alongside former Cavaliers sideline reporter and Lakers host [[Allie Clifton]] and teammate and close friend [[Channing Frye]]. Many of the podcast's first shows featured Jefferson's Cavs teammates and were recorded while on road trips.

In 2025, ESPN named Jefferson to its lead ''[[NBA on ESPN]]'' broadcast team along with fellow analyst [[Tim Legler]], play-by-play announcer [[Mike Breen]], and on-court reporter [[Lisa Salters]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://espnpressroom.com/us/press-releases/2025/08/espn-unveils-deep-roster-of-nba-game-commentators-for-2025-26-season/|title=ESPN Unveils Deep Roster of NBA Game Commentators for 2025-26 Season|last=Feuz|first=Alex|website=ESPN Press Room|date=August 28, 2025|access-date=October 22, 2025}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Jefferson dated dancer<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/GMA/story?id=8139244&page=1|title=Jilted NBA Bride: 'No Hard Feelings'|website=ABC News|last1=Ibanga |first1=Imaeyen |last2=Fortuna |first2=Roger |date=July 22, 2009}}</ref> and cheerleader<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/218257-richard-jefferson-leaves-bride-at-alter|title=Richard Jefferson Leaves Bride at Altar|first=Dumont|last=Walker|website=Bleacher Report|date=July 15, 2009}}</ref> Kesha Ni'cole Nichols for five years. They were engaged to be married on two occasions, but Jefferson broke off the engagement both times.<ref name="auto"/> The couple was scheduled to be married on July 11, 2009, at the Mandarin Oriental; however, Jefferson called off the wedding the night before it was scheduled to occur.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/entertainment/gossip/nba-star-richard-jefferson-dumps-bride-to-be-kesha-ni-cole-nichols-night-2-million-wedding-article-1.429025|title=NBA star Richard Jefferson dumps bride-to-be, Kesha Ni'Cole Nichols, night before $2 million wedding|first=Cristina|last=Everett|website=nydailynews.com|date=July 15, 2009}}</ref>

On July 11, 2022, the NBA announced that Jefferson would be a referee for the second quarter of the [[New York Knicks|Knicks]]–[[Portland Trail Blazers|Blazers]] game at the [[2022 NBA Summer League]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NBAPR on Twitter |url=https://twitter.com/nbapr/status/1546535043010424832 |access-date=2022-07-11 |website=Twitter |language=en}}</ref>
